title: Convoy MI-11, 30–31 July 1944
eyebrow: Luzon Strait · Coordinated Attack Group 17.15, Cdr L. S. Parks

participants.name: PARCHE
participants.co: Cdr L. P. Ramage; the group commander, Cdr L. S. Parks, aboard

paras.text: HAMMERHEAD found the convoy before dawn on 30 July, reported it to STEELHEAD and PARCHE at 0420 and attacked it from its port side at 0531 and 0537 (Tokyo time); STEELHEAD tracked it south all day and reported it to PARCHE. From 0332 on the 31st (Tokyo time) the two boats attacked it in turn off the north-west corner of Luzon; PARCHE made eight attacks in thirty-four minutes. The boats' war patrol reports beside the Navy's summary of the night, on one GMT clock.

The Navy's July summary: four ships sunk on the 31st (Yoshino, Manko, Fuso and Koei Maru, the last named plainly in the summary's fair copy) and two torpedoed and damaged (No. 1 Ogura Maru and Dakar Maru); the convoy withdrew for a time to Pangui Bay. No Japanese record found gives a time or place for any one ship, so which attack sank which is open: each claim is paired as possible in the boats' files. JANAC's postwar list puts three ships at PARCHE's position and two at STEELHEAD's, which are the boats' own; it has Dakar Maru sunk. HAMMERHEAD claimed one ship sunk and two damaged on the 30th; the summary's entry is for the 31st only.

Takao to Manila, sailed at 0500 on 29 July with sixteen ships and six escorts, carrying Army units and other transport. It had come south to Takao from 13 to 21 July. Its own record: [[convoy:mi-11]].

PARCHE, STEELHEAD and HAMMERHEAD formed Coordinated Attack Group 17.15 under Cdr L. S. Parks, who directed the boats from PARCHE (STEELHEAD's report, p11 and p50). GUARDFISH, sometimes put in this action, was in another pack (with PIRANHA and THRESHER under Capt. O'Regan); her report has her leaving the strait on 21 July and reaching Midway on the 31st.

Positions are the boats' own dead reckoning. Each typed one position for all its attack sheets: PARCHE 19-10N 120-58E, STEELHEAD 18-57N 120-50E, about 15 nm apart for attacks within the same hour, so at least one navigator was well off. PARCHE's narrative types no positions: her track is from her aircraft and ship contact tables. Lines between positions are straight.

All three boats kept zone I (−9) in the area, the same as the Japanese records (Tokyo time). PARCHE's last attack sheet types "0420-1433"; her narrative's 0429 and 0433 are used, with the typed times kept.

War patrol reports, NARA microfilm M1752 (PARCHE 74828617, STEELHEAD 74851415, HAMMERHEAD 74822943). The Navy's July 1944 summary (大東亜戦争経過概要（護衛対潜関係）) and the 1st Surface Escort Division's July war diary via JACAR (National Institute for Defense Studies). JANAC (1947), a postwar secondary list. Coastline: Natural Earth.

outcome.note: Six Mk 23 at 0531 I on 30 July at "the largest ship in the convoy", four hits, a passenger-freighter of the KANSAI MARU type claimed sunk, seen to sink by three men and its pip gone from the radar (rg367-74822943/p31). The summary has no loss on the 30th; it dates the convoy's attack from about 0330 on the 31st (J01, J02). The convoy still counted sixteen ships when the 31st's attack began, against HAMMERHEAD's count of fourteen, so the count can't show a ship lost on the 30th. One of the four ships the summary has sunk on the 31st could have been hit on the 30th, but the record doesn't say so

events.note: The Navy's day-by-day summary for July 1944 (大東亜戦争経過概要（護衛対潜関係）), the 31st. events.title: MI-11
events.words: The sixteen-ship convoy (six escorts) carrying Army units and other transport, which left Takao on the 29th for Manila, was attacked by submarines one after another from about 0330. Sunk: Yoshino Maru, Manko Maru, Fuso Maru, Koei Maru. Torpedoed and damaged: No. 1 Ogura Maru, Dakar Maru. The convoy withdrew for a time to Pangui Bay (the north-west tip of Luzon). [Beside it:] A submarine-hunting group formed, ?D x 6, concentrating (about 80 km) in cooperation [the last characters not certain]. [Below:] Since enemy submarines began to range over the Luzon Strait, the results hoped for have not yet been achieved

The convoy entry is the same text as J01-J03, so it counts once with them (a copy, not a second witness); it still gives no time or place for any one ship. What it adds: the fourth name written plainly as 光栄丸 (the first character as the 光 of 萬光丸 beside it), and two lines in the action column that the July summary's page (C16120659800 p9) doesn't have: a submarine-hunting group of six ("?D×6", the letter before D not read; perhaps escort vessels) formed to concentrate on the area, and a judgement that anti-submarine work in the Luzon Strait had not yet achieved what was hoped. The hunting group is not tied to MI-11 in the text. Event status: the losses are J02 and J03

paras.text: Takao to Manila, sailing at 0500 on 29 July 1944 with sixteen ships and six escorts. The ships carried Army units and other transport (the Navy's monthly summary for July, p9). From about 0330 on the 31st (Tokyo time) submarines attacked one after another; the summary gives no position. Four ships were sunk (Yoshino, Manko, Fuso and Koei Maru: the fourth name is cursive on the July page and written plainly 光栄丸 in the 2nd Demobilization Bureau's copy of the summary, p33) and two were torpedoed and damaged (No. 1 Ogura Maru, Dakar Maru). The convoy withdrew for a time to Pangui Bay at the north-west tip of Luzon. PARCHE and STEELHEAD attacked it that night, at about 19N 121E by their own reckoning. (The 1st Surface Escort's diary has a convoy "ミ一?" attacked off Cape Bolinao, some 150 nm further south; which convoy and which night are not yet settled.)

The convoy had come south to Takao before that: the 1st Surface Escort's chart has Shiokaze and Shimushu taking up (ミ一一) at 0600 on 13 July (Shimushu from Sasebo) and reaching Takao on the 21st, where it waited until the 29th.

The copy also notes, beside the entry, a submarine-hunting group of six formed (the type letter not read) and, below it, that since enemy submarines began to range over the Luzon Strait the results hoped for had not been achieved.

**Searched and not found** (5 Nov 2026): the six ships' names in the JACAR catalogue; the 4th Shipping Transport Command's Manila branch diaries, which on JACAR end in December 1943; the 31st Special Base Force's diary for July (the file holds September 1944 onward); No. 1 Ogura Maru or Dakar Maru in the Navy's August summary (C16120659900, a first read).
**Not yet found**: the other four escorts, the sixteen ships' names, the convoy's arrival at Manila, and each lost ship's own movement log (the hour and position of her loss).

words.remarks: Just prior to firing the Commanding Officer on the bridge requested the range. The reply was that the torpedo run was 2600 yards and as it was apparent target was diverging permission was granted to fire as a range of about 2400 yards. Actually the range was closer 3000 yards and the TDC set up was not correct as the targets were apparently still turning away. Ranges taken during and after firing showed this to be true and instead of a 2600 yard run the actual run was closer to 3200 yards. The time of the explosions bore this out. It is believed that the right hand torpedo in the spread was the one seen to hit the freighter and the left hand two torpedoes in the spread, hit the tanker.
